```{r setup}
library(tidydiversity)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Beta diversity measures how communities differ. Baselga (2010) showed that
dissimilarity has two parts: **turnover**, where species replace each
other, and **nestedness**, where poorer sites hold a subset of the species
at richer sites. The examples use `png_ants`, ants at nutrient baits along Mt Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea (Moses et al. 2023).

## Pairwise dissimilarity

```{r}
pairs <- beta_pair(png_ants, .by = season)
pairs
```

Turnover and nestedness add up to the total. Use `index = "jaccard"` for
the Jaccard family. The results match the betapart package.

```{r}
pairs |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(across(c(turnover, nestedness, total), mean))
```

## Many sites at once

```{r}
beta_multi(png_ants, .by = season)
```

## Distance decay

`beta_decay()` adds the distance between sites along a gradient. Here
turnover rises with elevational distance while nestedness stays low.

```{r}
decay <- beta_decay(png_ants, gradient = elevation, .by = season)
decay
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Dissimilarity against elevational distance"}
autoplot(decay)
```

## Beta diversity at equal sample coverage

Beta diversity estimated from samples depends on sample size and
completeness, so regions sampled with different effort cannot be compared
directly. `beta_hill()` follows the iNEXT.beta3D framework of Chao et al.
(2023): gamma and alpha Hill numbers are each standardised to the same
sample coverage, and beta = gamma / alpha is the effective number of
completely distinct sites (1 to the number of sites).

```{r}
beta_hill(png_ants, .by = season)
```

The four `dis_` columns rescale beta to 0-1. `dis_sorensen` and
`dis_jaccard` measure non-overlap (for q = 0 they are the classic
Sorensen and Jaccard dissimilarities); the `turnover` versions measure
species turnover. Give `coverage` to compare regions at chosen levels:

```{r}
beta_hill(png_ants, q = 0, coverage = c(0.8, 0.9), .by = season)
```

Add `nboot` for bootstrap confidence intervals. The same function gives
phylogenetic (`type = "PD"`, with `tree`) and functional (`type = "FD"`,
with `distance`) beta diversity, and works on incidence data with `unit`
when the same sampling units (plots, visits) were surveyed at every site.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
b <- beta_hill(png_ants, q = 0, coverage = 0.9, nboot = 20, .by = season)
b[c("season", "beta", "beta_lower", "beta_upper")]
```

Chao, A. et al. (2023). Rarefaction and extrapolation with beta diversity
under a framework of Hill numbers: the iNEXT.beta3D standardization.
*Ecological Monographs*, 93, e1588.
